lessons.title: Choosing Paints for Different Surfaces: Mud, Stone, Wood, Metal
lessons.body: Mud walls need breathable paint. Use lime wash or clay paint. Mix 1 part lime putty with 3 parts water. Add 1 cup of salt per 20 liters to help it stick. For stone, use silicate paint or lime wash. Stone is porous, so avoid plastic paints that trap moisture. Wood needs flexible paint. Use linseed oil paint or acrylic exterior paint. For new wood, prime with 1 part linseed oil and 1 part turpentine. Metal needs rust protection. Use red oxide primer first, then enamel paint. In Africa, the sun is harsh. Choose paints with UV inhibitors. For mud walls, test a small area first. If the paint peels, add more lime. For wood, sand lightly before painting. For metal, remove rust with a wire brush. Buy paint from local suppliers. In Kenya, Crown Paints and Basco are common. In Nigeria, Berger Paints. For traditional finishes, use natural pigments like ochre, charcoal, or cow dung. Mix with clay and water. These are cheap and locally available. Always check the label for drying time. Most paints dry in 2-4 hours in hot weather. Apply two coats for best results. Stir paint well before use. Never paint in direct sun or when rain is expected. For mud, apply in the morning when walls are cool. For metal, paint in the shade to avoid bubbles. Remember: the right paint saves money and lasts longer.

lessons.title: Surface Preparation: Cleaning, Sanding, Priming
lessons.body: Surface preparation is 80% of a good paint job. First, clean the surface. For mud walls, brush off loose dirt with a stiff broom. Mix 1 cup of vinegar in 5 liters of water to kill mold. For stone, scrub with a wire brush and water. For wood, wash with soapy water, then rinse. For metal, remove rust with a wire brush or sandpaper (80-grit). Wipe with turpentine to remove grease. Second, sand. For wood, sand with 120-grit paper, then 220-grit. Always sand with the grain. For metal, sand until shiny. For mud, smooth cracks with a mud and straw mix. Let dry for 2 days. Third, prime. Primer helps paint stick and blocks stains. For mud, use lime primer: 1 part lime, 2 parts water. For wood, use an oil-based primer. For metal, use red oxide primer. For stone, use a silicate primer. Apply primer with a brush. Let dry for 4-6 hours. In Africa, dust is a problem. Wet the ground before sweeping to keep dust down. Work in the shade. If you paint in the sun, the paint dries too fast and cracks. Always check for moisture. Press a plastic sheet on the wall for 24 hours. If moisture appears, wait. Never paint a damp wall. For wood, fill holes with wood filler. For metal, fill dents with epoxy. After priming, sand lightly with 220-grit. Wipe with a tack cloth. Now you are ready to paint. Good preparation means the paint lasts 5-10 years instead of 2.

lessons.title: Applying Paint: Brushes, Rollers, and Sprayers
lessons.body: Choose the right tool for the job. Brushes are best for small areas, corners, and detailed work. Use a 2-inch brush for trim and a 4-inch brush for walls. For mud and stone, use a wide brush with stiff bristles. For wood, use a soft brush. For metal, use a small brush. Rollers cover large areas fast. Use a 9-inch roller with a 10mm nap for smooth walls. For rough stone or mud, use a 20mm nap roller. Sprayers are fastest for big jobs. Use an airless sprayer for exterior walls. But sprayers need thinning. Add 10% water to acrylic paint. Always wear a mask when spraying. For brushes and rollers, use the 'wet edge' method: paint in 1-meter sections, then blend. Don't let the edge dry. For mud walls, apply paint in one direction. For wood, paint with the grain. For metal, paint in thin coats. Two thin coats are better than one thick coat. In hot weather, add a paint extender to slow drying. Mix 1 cup of glycerin per 4 liters of paint. For rollers, dip halfway, then roll on a grid. For brushes, dip one-third of the bristles. Tap off excess. Start at the top and work down. For sprayers, keep the nozzle 30cm from the surface. Move in steady lines. Overlap by 50%. Clean tools immediately. For water-based paint, wash with soap and water. For oil-based, use turpentine. Store brushes in a plastic bag in the fridge overnight. This saves cleaning time. Practice on a board first. A good painter uses less paint and gets a better finish.

lessons.title: Traditional Finishes: Earth Plasters and Natural Pigments
lessons.body: Traditional finishes are cheap, beautiful, and breathable. Earth plasters are made from clay, sand, and straw. Mix 3 parts clay soil, 1 part sand, and 1 part chopped straw. Add water until thick like peanut butter. Apply with a trowel or hand. First coat: 1cm thick. Let dry for 2 days. Second coat: 5mm thick. Smooth with a wet sponge. For a shiny finish, burnish with a stone or plastic trowel. Natural pigments come from rocks, plants, and insects. Ochre (red, yellow, brown) is found in many African soils. Charcoal gives black. Cow dung gives grey-brown. Mix pigments with clay slip: 1 part pigment, 2 parts clay, 3 parts water. Apply with a brush or rag. For a mottled look, use a sponge. For a solid color, apply two coats. In West Africa, people use 'banco' finish: mud, cow dung, and shea butter. In East Africa, 'lime wash' with ochre is common. These finishes last 2-5 years. They need reapplication after heavy rains. But they are free or very cheap. They also keep houses cool. To make lime wash: 1 part lime putty, 3 parts water, 1 cup salt per 20 liters. Add pigment. Apply with a brush. Let dry. For a water-resistant finish, add 1 cup of boiled cassava starch per 10 liters. Traditional finishes are good for mud and stone. Do not use on metal or wood. For wood, use linseed oil. For metal, use enamel. Always test a small area. If it rubs off, add more clay. If it cracks, add more sand. These finishes are part of African heritage. They are sustainable and locally sourced.

lessons.title: Protective Coatings for Weather Resistance
lessons.body: In Africa, weather is tough: sun, rain, dust, and wind. Protective coatings make buildings last. For mud walls, use lime wash with casein (milk protein). Mix 1 liter of milk with 1 liter of lime putty and 5 liters of water. This forms a water-resistant layer. Apply two coats. For stone, use a silicone-based water repellent. Brush it on. It lets stone breathe but stops rain. For wood, use linseed oil or polyurethane. Linseed oil is natural. Mix 1 part oil with 1 part turpentine. Apply three coats. Let dry 24 hours between coats. For metal, use epoxy or polyurethane paint. First, remove rust. Then apply red oxide primer. Then two coats of enamel. For roofs, use aluminum paint or bitumen. For walls, add a UV stabilizer to paint. In hot climates, white or light colors reflect heat. In rainy areas, use dark colors and add fungicide. For thatch, use a fire retardant. Mix 1 part borax, 1 part boric acid, and 10 parts water. Spray on. For concrete, use acrylic sealer. Apply with a roller. For all coatings, check the drying time. In humid weather, wait longer. In dry heat, work fast. Always wear gloves and a mask. Store coatings away from children. Reapply every 2-3 years. A good coating saves money on repairs. It also keeps the building cool in summer and warm in winter. Test a small area first. If it peels, try a different product. Local hardware stores stock these. Ask for 'weather guard' or 'damp proof' paint.

lessons.title: Hands-On: Painting a Small Building Exterior
lessons.body: Let's paint a small building exterior, step by step. You need: 20 liters of exterior paint, 5 liters of primer, 2 brushes (4-inch and 2-inch), 1 roller with 20mm nap, 1 roller tray, sandpaper (80 and 120 grit), a wire brush, a scraper, a ladder, a drop cloth, and a mask. First, clear the area. Move plants and furniture. Cover the ground with a drop cloth. Second, clean the walls. For mud, brush off loose dirt. For wood, wash with soapy water. For metal, remove rust. Let dry for 2 days. Third, repair cracks. For mud, fill with mud and straw. For wood, fill with wood filler. For metal, fill with epoxy. Sand smooth. Fourth, prime. Apply one coat of primer with a brush. Start at the top. Work in 1-meter sections. Let dry 4 hours. Fifth, paint. Stir the paint. Pour into a tray. Use a roller for large areas. Use a brush for corners and trim. Apply two coats. Let dry 4 hours between coats. For mud, use a brush only. For metal, use a brush. For wood, use a roller then brush. In hot sun, paint in the morning. In rain, wait. Sixth, clean up. Wash brushes with soap and water. Store paint in a sealed can. Check the finish. Look for missed spots. Touch up with a brush. Now your building is protected. It will last 5-10 years. You saved money by doing it yourself. You can teach others. Remember: preparation is key. Never skip priming. Always use two coats. Keep a small can of paint for touch-ups. Congratulations! You have finished Method 9.

quiz.q: What type of paint is best for mud walls?
quiz.explanation: Lime wash is breathable and allows moisture to escape from mud walls.

quiz.q: How much salt should you add to 20 liters of lime wash?
quiz.explanation: 1 cup of salt per 20 liters helps the lime wash stick to the surface.

quiz.q: What is the first step in surface preparation?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt, mold, and loose material so paint can adhere.

quiz.q: Which grit sandpaper is used for the final sanding of wood?
quiz.explanation: 220-grit gives a smooth finish before painting.

quiz.q: What is the best tool for painting a large flat wall quickly?
quiz.explanation: A roller covers large areas fast and evenly.

quiz.q: How much should you thin acrylic paint for a sprayer?
quiz.explanation: 10% water helps the paint flow through the sprayer without losing coverage.

quiz.q: What is a traditional earth plaster made from?
quiz.explanation: Clay, sand, and straw create a breathable, durable plaster.

quiz.q: Which natural pigment gives a black color?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal is a common black pigment in traditional finishes.

quiz.q: What is added to lime wash to make it water-resistant?
quiz.explanation: Casein (milk protein) forms a water-resistant layer.

quiz.q: How often should protective coatings be reapplied?
quiz.explanation: Weather and wear require reapplication every 2-3 years for best protection.

quiz.q: What is the first step when painting a small building exterior?
options: B) Clear the area and cover the ground
quiz.explanation: Clearing and covering prevents damage and makes cleanup easier.

quiz.q: How many coats of paint are recommended for exterior walls?
quiz.explanation: Two coats give better coverage and durability.

quiz.q: What should you use to remove rust from metal before painting?
quiz.explanation: A wire brush effectively removes rust and loose paint.

quiz.q: Which primer is best for metal?
quiz.explanation: Red oxide primer prevents rust and helps paint adhere to metal.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after priming before painting?
quiz.explanation: Primer needs 4-6 hours to dry in normal conditions.

quiz.q: What is the 'wet edge' method?
options: B) Painting in sections and blending before the edge dries
quiz.explanation: Blending wet paint into wet paint avoids lap marks.

quiz.q: Which additive slows down paint drying in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Glycerin acts as a paint extender, slowing drying in high heat.

quiz.q: What is 'banco' finish made from?
options: A) Mud, cow dung, and shea butter
quiz.explanation: Banco is a traditional West African finish using mud, cow dung, and shea butter.

quiz.q: How long does a traditional earth plaster typically last?
quiz.explanation: Earth plasters need reapplication every 2-5 years depending on weather.

quiz.q: What is added to lime wash to make it more water-resistant for mud walls?
quiz.explanation: Casein (milk protein) reacts with lime to form a water-resistant coating.

quiz.q: Which color reflects heat best in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: White reflects sunlight and keeps buildings cooler.

quiz.q: What should you add to paint in rainy areas to prevent mold?
quiz.explanation: Fungicide prevents mold and mildew growth in damp conditions.

quiz.q: How do you make a fire retardant for thatch?
options: A) Borax, boric acid, and water
quiz.explanation: A mix of borax, boric acid, and water is a common fire retardant.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store brushes overnight?
options: B) In a plastic bag in the fridge
quiz.explanation: A plastic bag in the fridge keeps brushes wet and ready for use.

quiz.q: How far should a sprayer nozzle be from the surface?
quiz.explanation: 30 cm gives an even coat without runs or gaps.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for painting a building exterior?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning first, then priming, then painting ensures good adhesion.

quiz.q: Which surface should NOT be painted with traditional earth plaster?
quiz.explanation: Earth plaster does not adhere well to metal and can cause rust.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a primer?
options: B) To help paint stick and block stains
C) To make paint dry faster
quiz.explanation: Primer seals the surface and improves paint adhesion.

quiz.q: How many liters of water are needed for a lime wash mix with 1 part lime putty?
quiz.explanation: The standard mix is 1 part lime putty to 3 parts water.

quiz.q: What should you do if paint peels after applying traditional finish?
quiz.explanation: Adding more clay improves adhesion and reduces peeling.
